questions.question: What is the key difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
options: Synchronous code runs one instruction at a time, waiting for each to finish; asynchronous code can start multiple tasks and handle results as they complete
Asynchronous code only works with databases
Synchronous code is always written in Python, asynchronous only in JavaScript
There is no real difference — it's just terminology
questions.explanation: Synchronous execution waits for each task to finish before starting the next; asynchronous execution can start several tasks and process each as it completes, avoiding idle waiting time.

questions.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Concurrency means managing multiple in-progress tasks over overlapping time (no extra CPU cores needed); parallelism means running multiple tasks at the exact same instant, requiring multiple cores
Concurrency only applies to databases, parallelism only to APIs
Parallelism is slower than concurrency in every case
questions.explanation: Async programming for API calls is typically about concurrency — juggling many 'waiting for a response' tasks efficiently on one worker — not true parallelism, which needs multiple CPU cores executing simultaneously.

questions.question: A team wants to make a slow batch-summarization feature 'fully async' by firing off 50 LLM calls at once. What is the best follow-up question to ask?
options: Can we just buy more RAM instead?
Will firing off 50 requests at once hit our RPM/TPM rate limits faster, and do we have backoff/retry or a concurrency limit in place?
Why do we need to summarize documents at all?
Can we switch the whole codebase to a different language?
questions.explanation: Async programming interacts directly with rate limits: firing off many requests simultaneously can hit RPM/TPM ceilings faster than a slow sequential approach, so a concurrency limit and backoff strategy are important safeguards.
